concepts/centralization-vs-bilateral.title: centralization-vs-bilateral
concepts/centralization-vs-bilateral.content:
Definition
Whether a market runs communication through a single neutral clearinghouse/datahub (centralized) or via direct point-to-point exchange between market actors (bilateral) — the single axis most of this ontology’s other concept notes end up measuring against.
Comparison across markets

germany — explicitly bilateral/decentralized; no national datahub; SMGW-level sovereignty by design; slower rollout (~15% iMSys penetration as of March 2025) attributed partly to this design choice plus strict Common Criteria certification requirements.
netherlands — confirmed centralized: EDSN (DSO+TSO cooperation platform, successor to Energy Clearing House, dating to 2001/2007) runs C-AR (switching) and C-ARM (allocation/reconciliation/metering) as shared national systems. ~94% smart-meter penetration, mandatory by Jan 2026 — fast rollout alongside centralization, echoing Japan’s pattern rather than Germany’s.
entsoe-cim — split answer: strictly TSO/wholesale-level centralization exists and is mature (CACM/EBGL/CIM), but retail-level harmonization was advisory-only (ebIX, 2002–2023) until Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 made a narrow slice (metering/consumption data access) binding EU-wide from Jan 2025. Not a datahub in the EDSN/Japan sense — a reference-model mandate, not an operated clearinghouse.
japan — centralized via a two-tier stack: 集約システム (national aggregation) + 電力データ管理協会 (single certified access intermediary); fast rollout, but consumer direct access and vendor concentration are the tradeoffs.

Patterns
The swing case resolved: EDSN-centralized Netherlands does achieve Japan-like rollout speed (~94% vs Japan’s near-100% Gen-1) without Japan’s most-criticized tradeoff — EDSN appears to combine the aggregator and access-point role in one DSO/TSO-owned cooperative rather than splitting it into a separate paying-intermediary layer the way Japan’s 電力データ管理協会 does (open question: whether NL has an equivalent access-fee/gating structure — not yet confirmed either way). This makes centralization-per-se look less causally tied to Japan’s specific access-friction tradeoff than the phase-1 hypothesis assumed — the friction may be a Japan-specific institutional choice (statute-mandated single private intermediary with its own fee schedule), not an inherent cost of centralization. Germany remains the clear bilateral/decentralized outlier, and its slower rollout is better explained by its Common-Criteria certification regime than by decentralization alone — worth stress-testing further. ENTSO-E adds a fourth pattern this axis didn’t originally anticipate: centralization can be layered — mature and binding at one institutional level (TSO/wholesale) while remaining advisory-then-newly-binding-and-narrow at another (retail data access) within the same overall system.

concepts/message-formats.title: message-formats
concepts/message-formats.content:
Definition
The actual wire/document formats used to exchange market-communication data — EDI standards, object models, APIs — independent of the business process they carry.
Comparison across markets

germany — UN/EDIFACT (D.03B) under EDI@Energy AHB/EBD governance; key types UTILMD, MSCONS, ORDERS, INVOIC, UTILTS, APERAK. Meter layer: DLMS/COSEM (dominant) with legacy SML.
netherlands — meter layer: DSMR, the Dutch national companion profile to DLMS/COSEM (confirmed “pull” mechanism over TCP) — converges with Germany here. Business messaging: historically EDINE (a distinct Dutch EDI dialect, not EDIFACT-energy proper) over the CPS secure-mail system, reportedly migrating to XML over AS4 via an “MMC-Hub” (lower-confidence, single-source claim). NL was an ebIX member 2002–2023.
entsoe-cim — two paradigms, not one: TSO-level CIM (IEC 61970/61968/62325, ESMP profile) — data-model-driven, structurally different from EDIFACT’s message-transaction paradigm. Retail-facing role/data model historically defined by ebIX’s Business Requirement Specifications (BRSs, ~38 of them), now owned by the EU DSO Entity/ENTSO-E Joint Working Group and partly codified as binding EU rule via Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 — built on ebIX/HEMRM/CIM concepts but not itself a full message-format mandate.
japan — ECHONET Lite (ISO/IEC 14543-4-3) at consumer interface instead of DLMS/COSEM; proprietary per-TDO/電力データ管理協会 APIs for data interchange; OCCTO EDI (Ver.3A) for the public-server retailer data leg.

Patterns
Meter-layer protocols converge more than business-messaging protocols: Germany and Netherlands both run DLMS/COSEM-family standards (EDI@Energy’s DLMS/COSEM vs DSMR), while Japan diverges completely with ECHONET Lite. Business-messaging is more fragmented than expected even among the “mainstream” markets — Germany’s EDIFACT and Netherlands’ EDINE are both EDI-family dialects but not the same dialect, and both trace lineage partly through ebIX without being identical outputs of it (Germany reportedly stayed on national EDIFACT despite ebIX membership — ebIX’s BRSs were advisory, not binding, until 2023/1162 changed that for the data-access layer specifically). ENTSO-E’s CIM is the clear outlier paradigm (object-model-driven vs transactional), and until Jan 2025 had essentially no binding reach into retail-market formats at all — Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 is the first real bridge, and it’s very recent, so its practical effect on national message formats (as opposed to data-access APIs) is still unverified.

concepts/metering-data-flow.title: metering-data-flow
concepts/metering-data-flow.content:
Definition
The path a meter reading takes from the physical meter to the parties that need it (DSO, supplier, consumer, third-party service providers) — including who aggregates it and at what latency/granularity.
Comparison across markets

germany — meter → SMGW (WAN/LMN/HAN interfaces) → MSB’s own Gateway Administration; no shared aggregation across MSBs; EMPs connect directly to a customer’s SMGW via HAN with cryptographic authorization.
netherlands — meter (DSMR P1/P2/P3 interfaces) → central data system → EDSN’s C-ARM (single national aggregation/reconciliation across all DSOs) → market-facing P4 retrieval point for suppliers/service companies. Genuine national aggregation, structurally between Germany’s no-aggregation model and Japan’s aggregation+consent-gate model.
entsoe-cim — not applicable at the TSO/CIM layer itself (grid-model/market data, not retail metering reads), but Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 now sets a binding EU reference model for how metering/consumption data access should work nationally — a harmonization pressure on this concept from above, not a data path itself.
japan — meter → per-TDO HES (real-time) → per-TDO MDMS → 集約システム (single national aggregation, 30-min push, 3-yr retention) → 電力データ管理協会 (consent/access gate) → utilization members.

Patterns
A three-point spectrum, not a binary: Germany pushes access authority down to the physical gateway (no aggregation, cryptographic per-device authorization); Netherlands aggregates nationally (EDSN/C-ARM) but without Japan’s extra consent-gating intermediary layer on top; Japan aggregates nationally and adds a separate certified-intermediary consent gate (電力データ管理協会) that Netherlands’ EDSN doesn’t appear to have an equivalent of — EDSN itself seems to be both the aggregator and the access point (P4), collapsing what Japan splits into two institutions. Worth testing directly: does EDSN’s dual role (aggregate + gate) create different competitive/access dynamics than Japan’s split model?

concepts/settlement-models.title: settlement-models
concepts/settlement-models.content:
Definition
How metering data becomes billed/settled volumes between market roles (DSO, supplier, TSO) — who aggregates readings, at what granularity, and via what clearing mechanism.
Comparison across markets

germany — DSO/MSB-centric, decentralized settlement; no central clearinghouse; 15-min granularity where deployed.
netherlands — genuinely centralized: EDSN’s C-ARM (Central Allocation, Reconciliation and Meter data) system does allocation/reconciliation for all DSOs. Smart-metered/interval connections settle on actual reads (15-min electricity, hourly gas); non-interval small consumers settle via NEDU standard consumption profiles (allocation, not measurement).
entsoe-cim — two separate layers, not one: TSO-to-TSO balancing/capacity settlement (CACM/EBGL) is genuinely EU-regulated via CIM/ESMP; retail supplier/customer settlement stays nationally defined, though EU Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 (binding since Jan 2025) now sets a common reference model for metering/consumption data access underneath national settlement.
japan — TDO-centric MDMS feeding single national aggregation layer (集約システム); 30-min standard settlement, Gen-2 adds 5-min for ≥10% LV.

Patterns
Centralization of settlement correlates with rollout speed and process simplicity (Japan’s near-100% Gen-1 rollout and NL’s ~94% smart-meter penetration vs Germany’s ~15% iMSys penetration as of March 2025), but Netherlands complicates the simple “centralize vs decentralize” binary: EDSN centralizes allocation/reconciliation while still relying on a profile-based fallback (NEDU) for consumers without interval metering — i.e. centralization of the clearing mechanism is separable from universal high-granularity measurement. Germany bet on decentralized-but-secure-by-design; Japan and Netherlands both centralized but arrived by different institutional routes (Japan: single certified private intermediary under statute; Netherlands: DSO/TSO-owned cooperation platform with a much longer institutional history, back to 2001/2007). ENTSO-E shows a third pattern: centralization exists but is scoped strictly to TSO-level settlement, with retail settlement staying national even as a thin EU-wide data-access layer (2023/1162) starts to standardize what sits underneath it.

concepts/switching-processes.title: switching-processes
concepts/switching-processes.content:
Definition
The mechanism by which a consumer changes energy supplier — which messages get exchanged, between whom, and whether it’s mediated by a central switch or bilateral EDI.
Comparison across markets

germany — bilateral EDIFACT process trees: GPKE (electricity), WiM (metering-point switching), GeLi Gas (gas). No central switch operator.
netherlands — confirmed centralized: EDSN’s C-AR (Central Connection Register) routes the switch message flow between old supplier, new supplier and DSO as a single national process, not bilateral EDI between the two suppliers.
entsoe-cim — not applicable in the strict sense (this layer doesn’t run retail switching), but since Jan 2025 EU Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 sets a binding reference model for the metering/consumption data access that switching-adjacent processes rely on — a first EU-level touch on the data underneath switching, if not the switching message flow itself.
japan — logical C-Route interface between TDO and retailer; meter stays with TDO (doesn’t change on switch), unlike UK where the supplier owns the meter.

Patterns
Meter ownership is a key variable shaping switching complexity: Japan/Germany/Netherlands all keep the meter with the network-side actor (TDO/MSB/DSO), so switching is a data/contract event, not a hardware event — this now holds across 3 of 4 seed markets. The real axis of variation turns out to be how the data/contract event is coordinated: Germany routes it peer-to-peer through defined EDIFACT process trees between exactly the parties involved in a given switch; Netherlands and Japan both route it through a shared national system (EDSN’s C-AR; Japan’s C-Route/TDO relationship) even though ownership structure differs sharply (DSO/TSO cooperative vs statute-backed private intermediary).

markets/entsoe-cim.title: entsoe-cim
markets/entsoe-cim.content:
Overview
ENTSO-E (European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity) coordinates transmission-level grid operation, cross-border capacity allocation, and balancing across ~40 European TSOs, using the IEC Common Information Model (CIM — IEC 61970/61968/62325) as its shared data language. Historically this layer stopped firmly at the TSO/wholesale boundary: retail-market harmonization (supplier switching, metering-data exchange between DSOs/suppliers/customers) was the job of a separate, much less institutionally powerful body, ebIX, which closed at the end of 2023 and handed its retail-facing role/data models to a new EU DSO Entity / ENTSO-E Joint Working Group. Since then, an EU-level binding rule — Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1162 (effective 5 January 2025) — has, for the first time, set an EU-wide reference model for metering/consumption data access, built explicitly on the ebIX/HEMRM/CIM lineage. This is a real (if narrow and recent) crack in the “TSO layer doesn’t touch retail” boundary that the previous stub version of this note assumed.
Standards body & governance
Three distinct bodies operate at this layer, each with a different mandate:

ENTSO-E — an association of European TSOs (Germany’s members: 50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW). It drafts network codes and technical CIM-based specifications (CGMES, ESMP) but does not itself have final regulatory authority.
ACER (Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators) — reviews and can revise ENTSO-E’s draft network codes/guidelines before submitting them to the European Commission with a recommendation. Under the revised Regulation (EU) 2019/943, ACER has the explicit right to revise (not just comment on) ENTSO-E’s drafts. The Commission adopts final network codes/guidelines as implementing or delegated acts via comitology.
European Commission — sets the three-year priority list for new network codes, formally requests ACER (framework guidelines) and ENTSO-E (draft code text), and holds final adoption authority. It can develop a code unilaterally if ENTSO-E fails to deliver.

Retail-facing harmonization sat outside this chain entirely until recently. ebIX (European forum for energy Business Information eXchange, founded 2002, growing out of the 1993 Norwegian Statnett Marked EDIFACT implementation guides and the 1995 Ediel Nordic Forum) was an independent, EU-unrecognized non-profit that wrote Business Requirement Specifications (BRSs, ~38 of them) covering nearly all downstream processes: supplier switching, change of grid company, measured-data exchange, consent administration. Its member countries were Austria, Belgium, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Slovenia, and Sweden. ebIX formally closed at end of 2023, judging its role superseded by the newly EU-mandated EU DSO Entity (created under Regulation (EU) 2019/943) and the Joint Working Group between the EU DSO Entity and ENTSO-E, which has adopted joint work plans for 2024–2025 and carries statutory responsibilities under Articles 11–12 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1162.
CIM’s own base standards (IEC 61970/61968/62325) are owned and maintained by IEC Technical Committee 57, working groups 13, 14, and 16 — a standards body independent of both ENTSO-E and the EU institutions, though ENTSO-E and (formerly) ebIX both fed change requests into it.
Protocol stack
Two genuinely separate stacks exist under the ENTSO-E/CIM umbrella, and conflating them was the main gap in the previous stub version of this note:
1. TSO/wholesale stack (mature, ENTSO-E-run):

IEC 61970 — power system/grid modeling (EMS, SCADA, network topology). ENTSO-E operationalized this as CGMES (Common Grid Model Exchange Specification), published 2013, mandated by EU regulators for TSO grid-model exchange from roughly 2015 onward.
IEC 61968 — distribution-side interoperability (asset/work management, customer information systems, metering) — the CIM branch that touches DSO-level systems, though it is a data-modeling standard for internal DSO IT integration, not a cross-border retail messaging mandate.
IEC 62325 — “Deregulated Market Communications.” Built on the 61970/61968 core object model, structured using UN/CEFACT’s Core Component Technical Specification (CCTS) methodology for deriving message profiles. Its European profile is the ESMP (European Style Market Profile), used for CACM (capacity allocation/congestion management), EBGL (balancing energy), and Transparency Platform reporting.

2. Retail/downstream stack (formerly ebIX, now JWG-owned):

ebIX’s own model was a UML model built with the UN/CEFACT Modelling Methodology (UMM) — a different modeling lineage than CIM’s UML, though both ultimately trace to UN/CEFACT conventions.
For roughly a decade before closure, ebIX ran a formal alignment project with IEC/TC57/WG16, submitting close to 100 Maintenance Requests since 2019 to get ebIX’s retail data elements represented in CIM, routed through an “ENTSO-E CIM for retail market work group” before final IEC approval. ebIX maintained its own CIM-derived layers: the European Style Downstream Market Profile (ESDMP) and various national CIM-based profiles.
ebIX’s BRSs were explicitly used as the specification basis for national retail data hubs in Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovenia, and Sweden — i.e., most of its member countries did converge their retail data-hub design on ebIX/CIM-derived models.
Germany is the visible exception: it was an ebIX member but built its retail market communication independently on EDIFACT/EDI@Energy (see germany) rather than an ebIX/CIM-based data hub, and has no central datahub at all. Membership in the harmonization body did not force convergence — participation was voluntary and advisory, not legally binding, until the 2023/1162 regulation.

3. The new binding layer (2025 onward): Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1162 (6 June 2023, effective 5 January 2025) establishes a mandatory EU-wide reference model — role model, information model, and process model — for access to metering and consumption data, covering roles like metered data administrator, metering point administrator, data access provider, and permission administrator. It explicitly reflects definitions and terminology from the ebIX-originated Harmonised Electricity Market Role Model (HEMRM) and IEC/CIM, and references IEC 62056 (DLMS/COSEM), EN 13757 (M-Bus), and other meter-facing standards for near-real-time data provision, while stating the reference model itself is “technology-neutral.” Member states had to report their national implementation practices to the Commission by 5 July 2025 for a public repository — this vault has not yet verified how far along that reporting/repository is as of August 2026, or whether Germany’s decentralized SMGW-gateway model is being treated as compliant.
Settlement & switching
Reassessing the stub’s “not applicable” claim: it was half right. There genuinely is no ENTSO-E/CIM-level retail supplier-switching process — that remains entirely national (Germany’s GPKE/WiM, etc.). But EBGL and CACM are real EU-level settlement regulations, not merely coordination frameworks: EBGL sets binding rules for balancing-energy settlement between TSOs (products, procurement, cross-border reserve sharing, and the settlement of balancing energy itself), and CACM governs capacity-allocation revenue distribution via implicit auctions in day-ahead/intraday coupled markets. These are TSO-to-TSO and TSO-to-market-operator settlement systems with legal force across the EU — a stronger claim than “harmonization layer above national markets,” which undersold it. The frontmatter above has been revised accordingly: settlement_model now distinguishes TSO-level settlement (genuinely EU-regulated) from retail settlement (still national). switching_process is revised similarly — no retail switching process exists here, but 2023/1162 does impose a binding EU data-access reference model that intersects with (without replacing) national switching processes.
Datahub / centralization
ENTSO-E operates the Transparency Platform (public data on generation, load, cross-border flows, outages) — a publication service, not a market-communication clearinghouse in the EDSN/DCC sense; it does not mediate transactional messages between market participants. At the retail layer, there is still no single EU datahub: national datahubs (where they exist, e.g. the Netherlands’ EDSN, several Nordic countries, Belgium) were built independently by each country, using ebIX BRSs as a common template rather than connecting to any shared European infrastructure. The 2023/1162 reference model does not create a central EU data hub either — it standardizes the model (roles, data objects, processes) that national data-access arrangements (centralized hub or bilateral) must expose, leaving the choice of centralized-vs-bilateral architecture to member states. Germany remains the clearest example of a member state implementing a fully decentralized (SMGW-gateway) model under this same EU umbrella.
Notable strengths / failure modes
Strength: the TSO/wholesale layer (CGMES, ESMP under CACM/EBGL) is a genuinely mature, mandatory, EU-regulated common data model with binding legal force via network codes/guidelines and real interoperability testing (ENTSO-E runs yearly CIM interoperability tests). This is a much stronger harmonization result than anything achieved at retail level.
Failure mode / structural gap: the retail-facing harmonization body (ebIX) was, for two decades, a voluntary, EU-unrecognized forum whose influence depended entirely on member goodwill — visible in Germany’s non-adoption of an ebIX-style datahub despite membership. Its 2023 closure created a real institutional risk (per ebIX’s own closure memo: loss of the UML model, UMM modeling knowledge, BRS maintenance capability, and CIM alignment expertise) that depended on a clean handover to the EU DSO Entity and Joint Working Group — a handover ebIX’s own memo flagged as not yet secured as of November 2023 (the EU DSO Entity had, at that point, declined to formally join the ebIX/EFET/ENTSO-E Harmonisation Group maintaining the HEMRM). Update (2026-08-16 pass): the gap is still not formally closed — the EU DSO Entity’s own 2026 work programme describes an “updated MoU between ENTSO-E and DSO Entity” as still “currently under development,” meaning the handover ebIX flagged in 2023 had not been formalized even three years later. No source found states exactly which expertise was or wasn’t absorbed in the interim.
Open structural question resolved: yes, this layer now does constrain (a slice of) national retail-market protocols — but only since January 2025, only for metering/consumption data access (not full switching-message formats), and via a route (ebIX → HEMRM → 2023/1162) that is organizationally distinct from ENTSO-E’s own CIM/62325 work, even though both ultimately reference the same IEC CIM base model.
Open questions

Current maturity of 2023/1162 national-practice reporting — partially resolved 2026-08-16: Article 10(4) confirms the 5 July 2025 deadline exactly as stated. Whether the resulting public repository is now live, and how complete member-state reporting actually is, remains not found — still open.
Whether the JWG has fully absorbed ebIX’s UMM/BRS expertise — resolved 2026-08-16 as still open, formally: an updated ENTSO-E/DSO Entity MoU is “currently under development” per the DSO Entity’s 2026 work programme, meaning the handover gap ebIX flagged in Nov 2023 hadn’t been formalized three years later.
CEEDS’s binding force and relationship to 2023/1162 — resolved 2026-08-16: CEEDS is not independently binding — the 3 June 2026 Strategic Roadmap anchors it as a coordination/architecture framework riding on already-binding regulation (2023/1162 plus upcoming supplier-switching/demand-response acts), not a new binding instrument itself.
CGMES/ESMP vs. retail reference model technical bridge — checked again 2026-08-16, genuinely not found (not just under-researched): no concrete technical bridge specification exists anywhere findable, only conceptual/terminology alignment via shared HEMRM vocabulary.
Whether/how the Netherlands’ EDSN (built on ebIX BRSs, confirmed — see netherlands) and the Nordics’ datahubs differ in their degree of CIM-native vs. CIM-adjacent implementation — flagged for the Netherlands and Nordic market notes, not resolved here.
ACER’s own website returned 404s — resolved 2026-08-16: acer.europa.eu is now live and directly confirms ACER’s 6-month network-code review/“reasoned opinion” role under Regulation 2019/943, matching the note’s existing secondary-sourced claim (now primary-sourced).

markets/germany.title: germany
markets/germany.content:
Overview
Germany runs energy market communication as bilateral EDIFACT messaging between market roles (supplier, DSO, MSB/metering point operator), governed by BDEW’s EDI@Energy framework under BNetzA oversight. No national data hub exists — every actor talks EDI directly to every other actor it needs. At the meter layer, the Smart Meter Gateway (SMGW) is the “sovereign” access point: each SMGW is its own decentralized access node rather than feeding a central intermediary.
Standards body & governance
EDI@Energy (run under BDEW, the German energy/water industry federation) owns the EDIFACT message formats and process definitions (AHB — Anwendungshandbuch, EBD — Entscheidungsbaumdiagramm). Process families are named per business flow: GPKE (Geschäftsprozesse Kunden-/Lieferantenwechsel Elektrizität — customer/supplier switching), WiM (Wechselprozesse im Messwesen — metering-point switching), GeLi Gas (gas supplier switching). BNetzA issues the underlying regulatory rulings (Beschlusskammern BK6/BK7) that make EDI@Energy’s specs binding. Smart-meter-specific technical security requirements sit separately with BSI (TR-03109 series) under the MsbG (Messstellenbetriebsgesetz).
Protocol stack
Market communication (switching, billing, metering data exchange) runs on UN/EDIFACT, version D.03B, structured by EDI@Energy AHB/EBD documents. Key message types: UTILMD (utility master data / switching), MSCONS (meter reading data), ORDERS/ORDRSP, INVOIC, UTILTS (gas time series), APERAK (error acknowledgment). At the physical meter layer, DLMS/COSEM (IEC 62056) is the dominant protocol, with SML (Smart Message Language) historically used for meter-to-SMGW LAN comms in Germany specifically, increasingly being displaced by DLMS. The SMGW’s three interfaces — WAN (to DSO/supplier/MSB), LMN (to meters), HAN (to consumer/CLS devices) — are all specified separately under BSI TR-03109.
Settlement & switching
No central settlement operator. Supplier switching and metering-point processes run through the GPKE/WiM/GeLi Gas EDIFACT process trees — a defined sequence of EDIFACT messages exchanged bilaterally between the old supplier, new supplier, and the responsible DSO/MSB. Each Metering Point Operator (Messstellenbetreiber, MSB — usually DSO-affiliated but contestable/competitive) operates its own Gateway Administration (GWA) for its SMGWs; there is no shared aggregation layer across MSBs.
Datahub / centralization
Explicitly rejected the centralized data-broker model. Data access is mediated at the SMGW itself — energy management providers (EMPs) can connect directly to a customer’s SMGW via the HAN interface with cryptographic authorization, rather than pulling from a national intermediary. This is the structural opposite of Japan’s 電力データ管理協会 single-intermediary model or the Netherlands’ EDSN model (per naming in seed scope — Dutch centralization not yet verified in this vault, see netherlands).
Notable strengths / failure modes
Strength: maximal decentralization and data sovereignty at the gateway — no single point of data concentration, cryptographic per-device authorization.
Failure mode: the same decentralization plus a strict Common Criteria certification regime (BSI-CC-PP-0073, ≥3 independent vendors required pre-GNDEW) caused a well-documented rollout stall through early 2025 — only ~15.1% of mandatory smart-meter cases had installed iMSys as of 31 March 2025. The GNDEW reform (April 2023 + Feb 2025 MsbG amendment) removed the three-vendor requirement; rollout then accelerated faster than this note originally assumed — BNetzA’s own quarterly statistics show 20.2% by Q3 2025 and 23.3% by Q4 2025, already past the 20% end-2025 target. A November 2025 industry study (Horizonte Group) does still flag risk ahead, but its actual claim is narrower than “milestones are unlikely to be met” generically: specifically, the 2026 target (90% of mandatory installations) is flagged as unachievable on current technical capacity — the note’s originally-cited 50%/2028, 95%/2030 staged GNDEW figures could not be independently re-confirmed and should be treated as unverified pending a direct GNDEW-legislation check.
Open questions

Exact current EDIFACT version in force (D.03B confirmed as of recent AHB releases, but should re-verify against latest EDI@Energy release calendar).
Whether/how CIM (IEC 62325) or ebIX cooperation touches German cross-border processes — partially resolved by entsoe-cim research: Germany was an ebIX member but stayed on EDIFACT/EDI@Energy rather than adopting an ebIX/CIM-derived national datahub, making Germany the visible non-convergence case among ebIX members. Since EU Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 (binding from Jan 2025) sets an EU-wide reference model for metering/consumption data access, whether Germany’s SMGW-gateway model is being treated as compliant is not yet verified.
SML vs DLMS/COSEM split at the SMGW LAN interface — no external source found with a concrete migration share or timeline (checked in the 2026-08-16 sourcing pass).
Current EDIFACT syntax version in force is unconfirmed — BNetzA’s “Allgemeine Festlegungen” process-document versioning (v6.1+) is distinct from the underlying UN/EDIFACT release, and the note’s “D.03B” claim may conflate the two. Needs a dedicated follow-up before marking verified.

markets/japan.title: japan
markets/japan.content:
Overview
Japan’s architecture is built around the 10 General Transmission & Distribution Operators (一般送配電事業者, TDOs), each owning meters and running its own MDMS/HES stack, feeding a single shared national aggregation layer (集約システム, built/operated by GDBL) and a single certified data intermediary (電力データ管理協会) that mediates all third-party access. Consumer-facing device communication uses ECHONET Lite rather than the internationally dominant DLMS/COSEM, making Japan a structural outlier among large industrialized markets.
Standards body & governance
ECHONET Consortium owns ECHONET Lite (ISO/IEC 14543-4-3) and runs SMA/AIF certification. Wi-SUN Alliance owns the 920MHz radio layer (IEEE 802.15.4g-based); TTC (Telecommunication Technology Committee) adopted Wi-SUN enhanced HAN as national standard JJ-300.10. The 10 TDOs coordinate through TDGC (送配電網協議会) for common specs (e.g. the 特定計量システム external-connection standard, common across all 10 TDOs). 電力データ管理協会 is a METI-certified body (認定協会 under Electricity Business Act Art.37-3/37-4, not bare Art.37) governing consent and third-party data access nationally.
Protocol stack
Japan’s field/radio layer is not one route but five, each with a different purpose and none of them interchangeable:









































RouteDirectionProtocolPurposeA-RouteMeter → TDO MDMSWi-SUN 920MHz multi-hop (IPv6)Utility reading, billing (the only route the previous draft of this note covered)B-Route LVMeter → HEMSWi-SUN ECHONET Lite + Wi-Fi 2.4GHz (Wi-Fi added in Gen-2)Consumer energy management — Japan’s structural analogue to Germany’s SMGW HAN interface or the Netherlands’ P1 portB-Route HVHV meter → BEMSWi-SUN B-RouteLarge commercial building energy managementC-RouteTDO → RetailerLogical inter-business (non-radio)Switching, settlement — carries OCCTO EDI, not field commsIoT-RouteMeter → Gas/Water/EV/PV sub-meters (特例計量器)Wi-SUN enhanced HAN 920MHz, TTC JJ-300.10 (ratified 16 May 2024)Cross-utility co-metering
IoT-Route’s full stack is documented in a March 2026 all-10-TDO external-connection guideline: L1–L4 (physical through transport) run IEEE 802.15.4 / 6LoWPAN / IPv6 / ICMPv6 / UDP per Wi-SUN Alliance spec, while L5–L7 (session through application) run DLMS/COSEM per a テレメータリング推進協議会 spec — meaning IoT-Route’s upper layers actually share a protocol family with European DLMS/COSEM metering infrastructure, giving DLMS-experienced vendors a directly transferable implementation path even though Japan’s core consumer interface (ECHONET Lite) does not use DLMS/COSEM. Security is comparably strict: IoT-Route mandates hard network isolation from A-Route and B-Route (no IP forwarding between routes), mutual authentication, and AES-128 minimum at Layer 2.
Consumer interface layer (all non-IoT routes): ECHONET Lite object model — global standard equivalent would be DLMS/COSEM (IEC 62056), which ~65% of non-China smart meters worldwide use; Japan, China, and the US are the major exceptions. Data format layer: two structurally separate, non-standardized paths rather than one EDIFACT-equivalent interchange format (contrast DLMS+OBIS codes, NEM12/13 in Australia, GBCS in UK, EDIFACT-energy in Germany) — OCCTO EDI Ver.3A for retailers (via C-Route/public-server, automatic, no consent) and 電力データ管理協会/SMDSA for any other qualifying entity (via a separate 集約システム→協会システム chain, consent-gated for individual data). See Settlement & switching below for how these two paths differ operationally.
Settlement & switching
Meter → TDO MDMS (Route A) → per-TDO HES (real-time) → MDMS (reading store/MDM + asset mgmt/AM + network mgmt/NM) → 集約システム (single national aggregation layer, 3-year retention, 30-min push from each TDO) → 電力データ管理協会 (consent/access management) → 利用会員 (utilization members, tiered by data type). Supplier switching and settlement run over the logical C-Route interface between TDO and retailer. Settlement granularity is 30-minute (Gen-1 and Gen-2 standard), with Gen-2 adding 5-minute collection for ≥10% of LV meters — later than Australia’s national move to 5-minute settlement (Oct 2021).
Two structurally distinct data-access paths exist beyond switching itself, and they don’t overlap:








































AspectOCCTO EDI Ver.3A (C-Route)電力データ管理協会/SMDSAEligible usersLicensed retailers onlyAny qualifying entity — retailers, DR aggregators, municipalitiesConsumer consentNo — automatic under the wheeling contractYes, for individual data (B1 tier)Statistical/aggregate dataNoYes (B2 tier, no consent needed)Sub-meter (特定計量, 機器点-level) dataYesNo — SMDSA scope stops at supply-point levelPricingCertification only (~¥5,200–9,800 one-time/2yr)¥200k–500k/yr membership + monthly/per-consent feesData sourceDirect from each TDO’s public serverVia the aggregated 集約システム → 協会システム chain
This means a DR aggregator or municipality with no retail license has exactly one legal path to individual meter data — 電力データ管理協会/SMDSA, gated behind ISMS certification (ISO 27001/27701) for the individual-data (B1) tier — while a licensed retailer gets faster, cheaper, consent-free access via OCCTO EDI but cannot get sub-meter (特定計量) data through SMDSA at all, since that stays a retailer-only OCCTO EDI product.
Datahub / centralization
Two-tier centralization: 集約システム is the single national data-aggregation layer across all 10 TDOs (public-private hybrid, GDBL-operated), and 電力データ管理協会 is the single certified national access/consent intermediary sitting above it. This is the most centralized model among the markets in this ontology so far — contrast Germany’s explicit rejection of any central intermediary (germany).
Notable strengths / failure modes
Strengths: near-100% Gen-1 rollout (fast vs UK/DE/US); IoT-Route is genuinely ahead internationally — no other country uses the electricity meter network as a shared data backbone for gas/water at national scale; 10-TDO common spec suppresses procurement fragmentation costs seen in the US’s 50-state model.
Failure modes: correction (2026-08-16): consumer direct data access is not structurally absent — B-Route LV (meter → HEMS, via Wi-SUN ECHONET Lite / Wi-Fi 2.4GHz) is exactly a consumer-direct real-time channel, Japan’s analogue to Germany’s SMGW HAN port. What is structurally absent is third-party (non-consumer, non-retailer) access without a paying intermediary — any DR aggregator, municipality, or building operator must go through 電力データ管理協会/SMDSA, gated behind ISMS certification and per-consent fees for individual data (an opt-out/access fee for individuals has been reported at ¥44,000 from April 2028, but this figure is unverified — 電力データ管理協会’s own published fee schedule only shows data-utilization-member tiers, ¥200k/yr statistics-only and ¥500k/yr+usage for individual data, not an individual consumer fee; needs its original source re-checked); concentration risk — TEPCO PG + Chubu + Kansai + NTT Data effectively control the only legal national data intermediary (GDBL, confirmed founded 26 Apr 2022); Gen-2’s 5-minute granularity arrives ~5 years after Australia’s equivalent move; ECHONET Lite isolation forces international meter vendors (Landis+Gyr, Itron, Sagemcom) to build Japan-specific variants.
Open questions

No message-format-level detail on 電力データ管理協会/OCCTO EDI structure — resolved 2026-08-16, see Settlement & switching table above.
The “JJ-300.10” TTC standard number and May 2024 IoT-Route ratification date are corroborated by vault-internal primary-source research (2026-08-16) but not by a fresh external fetch in this pass — Wi-SUN Alliance’s own public material confirms the technology and Japan-specific usage but not that exact standard number/date independently. One step short of a clean external verification.
Whether/how ECHONET Lite’s international isolation is likely to change. A Mitsubishi Electric × Landis+Gyr MoU (27 Jan 2026) exists, but the official announcement centers on Landis+Gyr’s Revelo sensor platform and North America — it does not mention ECHONET Lite or Japan-market interoperability, so it should not be read as a bridge for this specific isolation issue.
Full B-Route/IoT-Route distinction and 特定計量システム protocol detail — resolved 2026-08-16, pulled from vault (Japan Smart Metering/Sources/*) into this note’s protocol_layers and Protocol stack / Settlement & switching sections.
The B-Route HEMS/BEMS channel is now documented structurally (protocol, direction, purpose) but not researched in the depth A-Route and IoT-Route now have — no consumer-adoption rate, HEMS-market-penetration figure, or device-certification detail pulled in yet.

markets/netherlands.title: netherlands
markets/netherlands.content:
Overview
The Dutch market runs on a genuinely centralized architecture: EDSN (Energie Data Services Nederland), a cooperation platform of the country’s regional DSOs together with TSOs TenneT (electricity) and GTS/Gasunie (gas), operates the shared central systems that every other market actor talks to — rather than DSOs, suppliers and meter operators exchanging bilateral EDI as in Germany. EDSN was founded in 2007 as the successor to an earlier entity, Energy Clearing House (ECH), which itself dates the underlying central-switching model to at least 2001. This is the clearest “national datahub” pattern found across the markets researched so far in this vault, structurally closer to the UK’s DCC or Japan’s 電力データ管理協会 concept than to Germany’s fully bilateral EDI@Energy model.
Standards body & governance
EDSN is described consistently across secondary sources as a “cooperation platform of the network operators” (samenwerkingsplatform van de netbeheerders), working together with the regional DSOs, TenneT and GTS. Its legal form is confirmed as a B.V. (besloten vennootschap), KVK no. 39098825, Amersfoort — but no shareholder/ownership list was found on EDSN’s own site or in the registry excerpt checked, so the formal ownership question remains genuinely open (not just under-researched). ACM (Autoriteit Consument & Markt), the Dutch competition/markets regulator, supervises the energy market broadly: it licenses electricity and gas suppliers and sets the “energy codes” (binding technical/process rules) that govern network operators and suppliers — but ACM does not appear to operate EDSN itself; EDSN sits on the industry side, DSO-and-TSO-owned. Separately, NEDU (Vereniging Nederlandse EnergieDataUitwisseling), an industry association distinct from EDSN, owns the methodology for standard consumption profiles used in allocation — NEDU and Netbeheer Nederland (the DSO trade association) can also submit complaints/proposals affecting ACM’s codes.
Protocol stack
At the meter, the Dutch smart meter runs DSMR (Dutch Smart Meter Requirements), the national companion specification layered on DLMS/COSEM (IEC 62056) — the same underlying application-layer standard used in Germany and elsewhere, but with a Dutch-specific interface and behavior profile (confirmed: DLMS/COSEM’s “pull” mechanism over TCP is the model used, rather than a push model). The Dutch profile defines several named physical/logical interfaces (P1 through P4 in community/vendor documentation): a local consumer-facing serial port (P1) for in-home displays and loggers, an M-Bus interface for daisy-chaining gas/water sub-meters to the electricity meter as master (P2), a WAN uplink over cellular/Ethernet/PLC to the central data system (P3), and a server-side market-access interface (P4) that is not really “at the meter” at all but the retrieval point suppliers and service companies use against EDSN’s central data.
For business/market messaging, the historical Dutch approach used EDINE — a Dutch EDI dialect — exchanged over the CPS (Central Postbus System), a secure central mailbox system. Secondary sources describe an in-progress migration away from EDINE/CPS toward XML-based messages exchanged over AS4 (a modern, payload-agnostic B2B web-services exchange standard) via something called the “MMC-Hub” (Market-to-Market Communication Hub). Correction (2026-08-16 pass): what’s actually confirmed is narrower than a market-wide EDSN migration — it’s TenneT’s own EDINE→AS4/web-services transition specifically (started 2017, still described as in-progress as of a June 2021 source, no completion date found). The broader EDSN/market-wide framing in the original single-vendor-page source is not independently confirmed and was likely a conflation. The Netherlands was also a member of ebIX (European forum for energy Business Information eXchange) from 2002 until ebIX’s dissolution at the end of 2023 — and this lineage is now confirmed, not just plausible: EDSN itself publishes documents explicitly titled “Business Service” specifications following the ebIX BRS (Business Requirements Specification) framework. ebIX’s own work, post-dissolution, transferred mainly to the EU DSO Entity and partly to a joint ENTSO-E/EU DSO Entity working group.
Settlement & switching
Switching (leverancierswissel) is centrally routed through EDSN rather than negotiated bilaterally between the losing and winning supplier. EDSN’s C-AR (Central Connection Register) system is described as managing the retail-side processes — address changes, supplier switches — forwarding the relevant electronic messages to and from the appropriate parties (old supplier, new supplier, DSO), including passing meter readings taken at the switch date to both suppliers and passing the data needed to calculate the new supplier’s advance payment/purchase requirements.
Settlement and allocation run through a second EDSN system, C-ARM (Central Allocation, Reconciliation and Meter data), which is reported to process meter data for more than 15 million Dutch electricity and gas metering points, handling peak volumes above 4 million meter-data messages per day, and performing daily allocation at 15-minute resolution for electricity and hourly resolution for gas. Where a connection lacks granular (interval) metering — the historical default for small consumers before smart-meter rollout, and still relevant for any unmetered/estimated cases — volumes are instead allocated to suppliers using NEDU’s standard consumption profiles, a statistically modeled shape of typical consumption rather than an actual per-interval read.
Datahub / centralization
EDSN is the datahub in the fullest sense found so far in this vault: it is not merely a message-routing/clearing intermediary (like a simple postbox) but appears to actively aggregate, allocate and reconcile metering data centrally via C-ARM, in addition to running the centralized switching process via C-AR. This is a stronger form of centralization than a pure message-clearing hub, and structurally the clearest opposite pole to Germany’s deliberately decentralized, no-datahub, gateway-sovereign model (see germany).
Notable strengths / failure modes
Not independently researched to the point of a confident assessment. Provisionally: the centralized C-AR/C-ARM model plausibly gives the Netherlands a single, consistent view of allocation and switching state (avoiding Germany-style multi-party reconciliation disputes), at the cost of EDSN itself being a single point of operational dependency for the entire market — but no incident history, outage record, or independent critique was found in this research pass to substantiate either side beyond structural inference. Flagged for a future pass rather than asserted.
Open questions

EDSN’s exact legal/corporate form — resolved 2026-08-16: B.V. (besloten vennootschap), KVK no. 39098825, Amersfoort. Formal shareholder/ownership list still not found — remains open.
Whether the EDINE→XML/AS4/MMC-Hub migration is EDSN/market-wide — resolved 2026-08-16: it’s confirmed as TenneT’s own transition (started 2017, in-progress as of a June 2021 source), not confirmed market-wide. The original single-vendor-page source likely conflated the two.
Whether NL’s business-messaging models are formally ebIX-derived — resolved 2026-08-16: confirmed. EDSN publishes documents explicitly titled “Business Service” specs following the ebIX BRS framework.
Exact current DSMR version in force — resolved 2026-08-16: there is no single mandatory baseline. DSMR 5.0.2 (2016) is current for new installs; DSMR 4.2.2 remains separately live/maintained. The field is mixed, not migrated to one version.
Whether EDSN’s role extends to gas the same way as electricity — resolved 2026-08-16: EDSN’s own site confirms it handles both electricity and gas; no evidence of GTS running a fully separate parallel system, though the operational split isn’t itemized in detail.
No incident/failure-mode history found (re-checked 2026-08-16, still nothing) — Notable strengths/failure modes section above remains structural inference only, not sourced fact.
No CIM (IEC 62325) adoption found at NL’s data-model layer (re-checked 2026-08-16) — protocol_layers.data_model remains status: stub.
Relationship between EDSN/NEDU allocation methodology and ENTSO-E/CIM harmonization layer, see entsoe-cim — not researched.

ontology-map.title: ontology-map
ontology-map.content:
Ontology Map
Two views of the same four markets: the protocol stack layer-by-layer, and the centralization/harmonization structure. Both render as Mermaid diagrams.
Protocol stack, layer by layer
Solid boxes = status: drafted. Dashed/grey boxes = status: stub. Directly reflects each market note’s protocol_layers frontmatter — if this diagram and a market note’s frontmatter disagree, the frontmatter is correct and this diagram is stale; re-run _templates/validate_ontology.py after fixing either.
graph BT
  subgraph DE["Germany — bilateral, no datahub"]
    DE_field["field_comms<br/>not separately specified"]
    DE_meter["meter_interface<br/>DLMS/COSEM + legacy SML"]
    DE_biz["business_messaging<br/>EDIFACT D.03B / EDI@Energy"]
    DE_data["data_model<br/>none distinct identified"]
    DE_field --> DE_meter --> DE_biz --> DE_data
  end

  subgraph NL["Netherlands — EDSN centralized"]
    NL_field["field_comms<br/>DSMR P2 (M-Bus) / P3 (WAN)"]
    NL_meter["meter_interface<br/>DSMR / DLMS-COSEM"]
    NL_biz["business_messaging<br/>EDINE/CPS → AS4/MMC-Hub"]
    NL_data["data_model<br/>NEDU consumption profiles"]
    NL_field --> NL_meter --> NL_biz --> NL_data
  end

  subgraph JP["Japan — two-tier centralized"]
    JP_field["field_comms<br/>Wi-SUN 920MHz"]
    JP_meter["meter_interface<br/>ECHONET Lite"]
    JP_biz["business_messaging<br/>proprietary APIs / OCCTO EDI"]
    JP_data["data_model<br/>ECHONET Lite object model"]
    JP_field --> JP_meter --> JP_biz --> JP_data
  end

  subgraph EU["ENTSO-E / EU — TSO layer, no meter reach"]
    EU_biz["business_messaging<br/>CIM/62325 ESMP + Reg. 2023/1162"]
    EU_data["data_model<br/>CIM 61970/61968/62325"]
    EU_biz --> EU_data
  end

  classDef drafted fill:#3f7d6a,stroke:#2b5a4c,color:#fff
  classDef stub fill:#9a9a9a,stroke:#767676,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 4 3
  class DE_meter,DE_biz,NL_field,NL_meter,NL_biz,JP_field,JP_meter,JP_biz,JP_data,EU_biz,EU_data drafted
  class DE_field,DE_data,NL_data stub

Centralization & harmonization structure
The core cross-market finding, as a picture: Germany is deliberately bilateral; Netherlands and Japan both centralized but via different institutional routes (cooperative datahub vs. statute-mandated paid intermediary); ENTSO-E sits above the EU members as a TSO-level layer that only recently (Jan 2025) started reaching down into retail data-access rules.
graph TB
  EU["EU layer<br/>ENTSO-E/CIM — TSO, mature<br/>ebIX → Reg. 2023/1162 — retail data-access, binding since Jan 2025"]
  DE["Germany<br/>bilateral EDIFACT, no datahub<br/>~15% iMSys rollout (Mar 2025)"]
  NL["Netherlands<br/>EDSN: C-AR + C-ARM<br/>DSO/TSO cooperative datahub<br/>~94% smart-meter rollout"]
  JP["Japan<br/>集約システム + 電力データ管理協会<br/>statute-mandated intermediary, access fee<br/>~100% Gen-1 rollout"]

  EU -. binding data-access reference model .-> DE
  EU -. ebIX BRS lineage shaped datahub design .-> NL

  DE --- NL
  NL --- JP

  classDef centralized fill:#3f7d6a,color:#fff,stroke:#2b5a4c
  classDef overlay fill:#33587a,color:#fff,stroke:#23405c

sources/acer-entsoe-network-code-process.title: ACER/ENTSO-E network code process (emissions-euets.com)
sources/acer-entsoe-network-code-process.content: Secondary/explainer source (not ACER’s or ENTSO-E’s own site, both of which 404’d on the specific pages fetched during this research pass — see Open Questions in entsoe-cim). Cross-checked against ENTSO-E’s own network-codes-implementation page (see entsoe-network-codes-and-cim source note), which independently confirms ENTSO-E’s drafting role and the CACM/EBGL scope description. Used for the ACER-specific procedural detail (framework guidelines, revision authority, Commission’s comitology adoption) that ENTSO-E’s own site did not spell out. Should be re-verified against ACER’s official site or the underlying Regulation (EU) 2019/943 text in a future pass.

sources/bdew-bnetza-bsi-germany-primary.title: BDEW/EDI@Energy, BNetzA, and BSI primary sources for German market communication
sources/bdew-bnetza-bsi-germany-primary.content:
Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-16. Confirms BDEW/EDI@Energy as AHB/EBD owner and BNetzA BK6 as the binding-regulation authority for GPKE/WiM; confirms BSI TR-03109 and the WAN/LMN/HAN SMGW architecture; confirms BSI-CC-PP-0073 as the correct Protection Profile ID.
Two claims in germany.md do not hold up and need correction:

EDIFACT version: could not confirm current format version is still D.03B. BNetzA’s “Allgemeine Festlegungen” documents are versioned separately (v6.1+) from the underlying UN/EDIFACT syntax release — these are different version numbers and the original note may have conflated them. Needs a dedicated follow-up, not marked verified here.
SML→DLMS/COSEM migration share: no source found with a concrete migration share or timeline. General protocol descriptions exist; no migration-progress data.

One claim is materially outdated and corrected: the note frames the iMSys rollout as “a well-documented rollout stall” with the 20% end-2025 target “widely expected to be missed” (citing 15.1% as of 31 March 2025). BNetzA’s own quarterly statistics show the rollout accelerated through 2025: Q3 2025 = 20.2%, Q4 2025 = 23.3% — the 20% end-2025 target was already exceeded by Q3. The rollout-stall framing describes the situation as of March 2025 but is stale as a characterization of where things stood by year-end. Separately, the Horizonte-Group (Nov 2025) study’s actual claim is narrower than the note states: it says the 2026 target (90% of mandatory installations) specifically is unachievable due to technical constraints — not “2026 milestones” generically — and no source was found confirming the note’s specific 50%/2028, 95%/2030 staged GNDEW figures.

sources/ceeds-common-energy-data-space.title: Common European Energy Data Space (CEEDS)
sources/ceeds-common-energy-data-space.content: Web search + WebFetch summary of European Commission digital-strategy pages and a related stakeholder-event page. CEEDS’s exact binding force, relationship to the already-binding Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1162, and concrete rollout timeline beyond “ongoing deployment phase” could not be established with confidence in this research pass — left as an explicit open question in entsoe-cim rather than guessed at. This source note should be revisited directly against the July 2024 blueprint document and June 2026 roadmap text if a firmer status update is needed later.

sources/ebix-nedu-market-messaging.title: ebIX (Wikipedia), NEDU, and EDINE/AS4/MMC-Hub messaging transition
sources/ebix-nedu-market-messaging.content: Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-15. The EDINE/CPS-to-XML/AS4/MMC-Hub claim rests on a search-engine-summarized snippet of a vendor page (egssis.com / energyone.com) whose full text could not be independently re-fetched (page migrated/redirected, content not confirmed on re-fetch) — treat as drafted/lower-confidence, flagged in Open Questions. ebIX membership and dissolution/successor claims are corroborated by Wikipedia’s EbIX article. NEDU’s profile-allocation role is corroborated by an independent vendor case-study (CQM) and an ACM code-change proposal document referencing “profielallocatie.” No verbatim spec text reproduced.

sources/ebix-organisation-and-closure.title: ebIX organisation, IEC alignment, and 2023 closure memo
sources/ebix-organisation-and-closure.content: Primary source: ebIX’s own “Memo: Consequences of closure of ebIX” (approved by ebIX Forum, 24 Nov 2023, PDF fetched and read directly — not transcribed verbatim into the market note, only facts extracted) plus ebIX.org’s organisation and IEC-alignment-project pages and the Wikipedia summary (cross-checked, not treated as sole source). The closure memo is the single most load-bearing document for this market note: it directly states ebIX’s BRSs were used as the specification basis for national data hubs in Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovenia, and Sweden, and documents the ebIX/IEC-TC57/WG16 alignment project (maintenance requests to CIM). It also records that as of Nov 2023 the EU DSO Entity had not yet agreed to join the Harmonisation Group maintaining HEMRM, flagging handover risk. ebIX’s own site states all its documents remain published until end of 2026.

sources/echonet-wisun-meti-japan-primary.title: ECHONET Consortium, Wi-SUN Alliance, TDGC, METI, and OCCTO primary sources for Japanese market communication
sources/echonet-wisun-meti-japan-primary.content:
Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-16. Confirms the core architecture claims in japan.md: ECHONET Lite/AIF certification, Wi-SUN 920MHz field layer, the 10-TDO/TDGC structure, and GDBL’s four-party ownership.
Corrections to japan.md:

Legal basis: the note cites bare “Art.37” for 電力データ管理協会’s certification. The actual basis is Electricity Business Act Art. 37-3 (data provision) / Art. 37-4 (certified association) — more specific than the note states.
Mitsubishi Electric × Landis+Gyr MoU (27 Jan 2026): real, but the official announcement is a general grid-edge/App-Ecosystem partnership centered on Landis+Gyr’s Revelo sensor platform and North America — none of the official material mentions ECHONET Lite or Japan-market interoperability. The note’s framing of this as a “partial bridge” for ECHONET Lite’s international isolation is not supported by what’s findable and should be softened or dropped.
¥44,000 opt-out fee (April 2028): not found. The official 電力データ管理協会 fee schedule shows data-utilization-member tiers (¥200k/yr statistics-only, ¥500k/yr+usage for individual data) — nothing matching an individual consumer opt-out fee at that figure. Flag as unverified, possibly conflated with a different fee; needs its original source re-checked.

Minor wording note: Gen-2’s granularity rule is more precise than “≥10% of LV meters get 5-minute collection” — METI’s 次世代スマートメーター report specifies ≥10% of low-voltage meters deliver 5-min data within days and ≥3% within 10 minutes. Worth tightening the note’s phrasing, not a factual error.
Not independently confirmed: the specific “JJ-300.10” TTC standard number and the May 2024 IoT-Route ratification date — Wi-SUN Alliance’s own material confirms the technology and Japan-specific usage but not that exact standard number/date.

sources/edsn-official-and-industry-profi.title: EDSN official site and industry profiles (governance, C-AR/C-ARM systems)
sources/edsn-official-and-industry-profi.content: Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-15. EDSN’s own marketing/informational pages are thin on formal governance detail (no explicit shareholder list or legal-form confirmation found in the fetched pages); the CGI case study is the most concrete technical/scale description found (C-AR, C-ARM naming, message volumes, allocation resolution). ACM’s own site confirms its regulatory role (licensing suppliers, setting energy codes) but was not fetched in full — role summarized from search snippets only. No verbatim spec or contract text reproduced; all paraphrased.

sources/edsn-tennet-nbn-netherlands-prim.title: EDSN legal form, ebIX BRS lineage, and DSMR version primary sources
sources/edsn-tennet-nbn-netherlands-prim.content:
Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-16. Resolves several open questions on netherlands.md, and corrects one conflation.
Confirmed:

EDSN’s legal form is a B.V. (besloten vennootschap), KVK no. 39098825, based in Amersfoort. No shareholder/ownership list was found on EDSN’s own site or in the registry excerpt — this remains genuinely open, not just under-researched.
EDSN itself publishes documents explicitly titled “Business Service” specifications following the ebIX BRS (Business Requirements Specification) framework — the ebIX-lineage question is resolved, not merely plausible.
EDSN’s own “over ons” page states it handles data for both electricity and gas; no evidence found of GTS (gas TSO) running a fully separate parallel system, though EDSN’s site does not itemize the electricity/gas split in operational detail.

Corrected — EDINE→AS4/MMC-Hub migration: the original note frames this as an EDSN/market-wide business-messaging migration. What was actually found is narrower: it’s TenneT’s own EDINE→AS4/web-services transition (started 2017, still described as in-progress as of a June 2021 source; no completion date located). This is likely a conflation in the note’s original single-vendor-page sourcing — the market-wide EDSN migration claim is not independently confirmed and should be treated as narrower in scope than originally stated.
Corrected — DSMR version: there is no single “current mandatory baseline.” DSMR 5.0.2 (Netbeheer Nederland, published 2016) is the current spec for new installs, but DSMR 4.2.2 remains a separately-maintained, still-live publication — the field is mixed rather than having migrated to one version.
Still not found: any publicly documented EDSN/C-AR/C-ARM outage, incident, or independent critique; any confirmation of CIM (IEC 62325) adoption at NL’s data-model layer beyond NEDU’s consumption-profile methodology.

sources/eu-dso-entity-acer-ceeds-primary.title: EU DSO Entity, ACER, and CEEDS implementation-maturity primary sources
sources/eu-dso-entity-acer-ceeds-primary.content:
Web research pass, accessed 2026-08-16. Resolves/updates the five open questions on entsoe-cim.md.
Confirmed as stated: 2023/1162 Article 10(4) matches the note’s existing 5 July 2025 reporting-deadline claim exactly. Whether the resulting public repository is now live, and how complete member-state reporting actually is, remains genuinely not found — no source located either way.
Handover gap still open: ebIX’s November 2023 closure memo flagged the EU DSO Entity/ENTSO-E handover of UMM modeling methodology and BRS-maintenance capability as not yet secured. As of 2026, an “updated MoU between ENTSO-E and DSO Entity is currently under development” per the DSO Entity’s own 2026 work programme — implying the gap ebIX flagged in 2023 still had not been formally closed three years later. No direct statement was found of exactly which expertise was or wasn’t absorbed in the interim.
CEEDS is not independently binding: the 3 June 2026 “Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector” anchors CEEDS as a governance/coordination framework, but the actual binding legal instruments cited are 2023/1162 (already known) plus upcoming acts on supplier switching and demand response. CEEDS reads as architecture riding on top of already-binding regulation, not a new binding instrument in its own right.
No technical bridge specification found (item 4) — genuinely unresolved, not just under-researched. Only conceptual/terminology alignment (shared HEMRM vocabulary) is documented anywhere findable between the TSO-layer CGMES/CIM message formats and the 2023/1162 retail reference model.
ACER’s site is live (correcting the prior 404s) and independently confirms ACER’s role: it reviews and can revise ENTSO-E’s draft network codes within a 6-month window under Regulation 2019/943, issuing a “reasoned opinion” before Commission submission — matching what the note already stated from a secondary source, now upgraded to primary-sourced.

sources/eu-implementing-regulation-2023-.title: EU Implementing Regulation 2023/1162 on metering/consumption data interoperability
sources/eu-implementing-regulation-2023-.content: Primary source: the regulation’s own text on EUR-Lex (fetched via WebFetch, facts extracted and paraphrased, not transcribed verbatim — EU legislative text is public domain but the market note describes structure/purpose in the vault’s own words per this vault’s sourcing rules). This is the concrete legal instrument that answers the note’s central open question (“does the ENTSO-E/CIM layer constrain national retail protocols?”) — the answer is: not directly through ENTSO-E/CIM itself, but through this separate Commission Implementing Regulation, which draws on the same HEMRM/CIM lineage that ebIX spent a decade building. Implementation maturity as of August 2026 (post the 5 July 2025 national-practice reporting deadline) was not independently verified in this pass — flagged as an open question.
